title: How does a chain of amino acids become a trait, and why can the same genes give different results?
subtitle: A ribosome builds a chain of amino acids. How does that chain become a trait you can see, and why can the same genes give different results?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: Name five jobs proteins do, explain why a chain folds into one shape and the four levels of structure, explain why shape decides function and why a changed amino acid can but need not change it, trace sickle cell from one base change to the trait, say why genes becoming traits directly skips steps, define genotype and phenotype, explain a same-genotype different-phenotype case, assess genes and environment together, analyse why polypeptide synthesis matters, and apply all of it to a temperature-sensitive enzyme and to two base changes read from a codon chart.

voiceover.text: A gardener takes cuttings from one hydrangea, so every new plant is a clone, with exactly the same genes. Planted in two different gardens, one flowers blue, and one flowers pink. Last time, a ribosome built a chain of amino acids. So how does a chain like that become a trait you can see, and how can the same genes give different results?

Most of a cell's jobs are done by proteins. Enzymes speed up reactions. Transport proteins carry things, like haemoglobin carrying oxygen in red blood cells. Structural proteins give strength, like the keratin in your hair. Receptors on a cell's surface pick up signals, and antibodies grab onto germs. Every one of these is built from one or more polypeptide chains, folded into its own shape.

So why does a chain fold into one particular shape? Because the twenty amino acids are different. Some avoid water, so they tuck into the middle of the chain, away from the watery cell. Some carry a charge, and opposite charges attract. And two amino acids called cysteine can lock together with a strong link called a disulfide bond. The order of amino acids decides which parts end up next to each other, so it decides the shape.

Shape matters because proteins work by fitting. An enzyme's substrate fits into a pocket, its active site, like a key in a lock, though the protein can flex a little as it binds. Change one amino acid in that pocket, and the shape can change so the substrate no longer fits. But not every change matters. A swap far from the pocket, or to a similar amino acid, may leave the shape working. And many base changes don't change the amino acid at all.

Let's follow one real case all the way. Haemoglobin is built from four chains. In the gene for one of them, the beta chain, a single base change turns the codon G A G into G U G in the mRNA. The chart gives valine instead of glutamate, at the sixth amino acid. So one base changes one amino acid, out of a chain of a hundred and forty-six.

Glutamate carries a charge, but valine avoids water. So in a person with two copies of this allele, when oxygen is low, the changed haemoglobin molecules stick to each other and stack into long stiff fibres. The fibres bend the red blood cells into a sickle shape. Sickle cells are stiff, so they block small blood vessels and cause pain, and they break down quickly, so there are too few red cells. That whole pattern is the trait, sickle cell disease.

Notice how many steps that took. Genes don't become traits directly. A gene codes for a polypeptide, which folds into a protein, which changes what a cell does, and that shows up as a trait. Your set of alleles is your genotype. The traits you can observe, from a cell's shape to the colour of a flower, are your phenotype. And most traits involve many proteins, so many genes, at once.

Now back to the hydrangeas. Their genes code for the enzymes that make a red pigment in the flowers. In acidic soil, aluminium dissolves, and the roots take it up. In the flowers, aluminium binds to the pigment and turns it blue. In less acidic soil, little aluminium dissolves, so the same pigment stays pink. The genotype is the same. The environment changes what it produces. Height works the same way. It depends on many genes, but children who don't get enough food don't reach the height their genes allow.

So how much is genes, and how much is environment? Genes set what's possible, and the environment affects what actually develops within that range. The balance differs between traits. Your ABO blood group is set by your alleles, and food or climate won't change it. Height depends on both. And the environment changes the trait, not the genes themselves. Take a cutting from the blue plant and grow it in less acidic soil, and its new flowers come out pink.

That's why making polypeptides matters so much. Almost everything a cell does depends on its proteins, and every protein is made by transcription and translation. Your cells all carry the same genes, but each kind of cell makes its own set of proteins, which is why a red blood cell fills with haemoglobin as it develops, and a muscle cell doesn't. If the sequence is wrong, or the protein isn't made, the job doesn't get done.

Two aids. For protein structure: one, the order of amino acids; two, local coils and folds; three, the whole folded shape of one chain; four, more than one chain together, like haemoglobin. And for traits: genes set what's possible, and the environment affects what actually develops.

Two harder questions now. First, Himalayan rabbits have white fur on the body, but dark fur on the ears, nose, feet and tail. The dark pigment is made by an enzyme. Scientists shaved a patch on one rabbit's back and kept an ice pack on it while the fur grew back. The new fur grew dark. Explain why the new fur is dark. Then predict the back fur of its young, which also have the Himalayan genotype and are raised normally, and justify your prediction. Pause here to answer.

The dark parts are the coolest parts of the body, so the enzyme must work only where the skin is cool. On the warm back it doesn't work, so no pigment forms. The ice pack cooled the skin, the enzyme worked, and the fur grew dark. The young will have white backs, because the cold changed where the enzyme worked, not the gene they inherit. If you said the ice changed the rabbit's genes, look again.

Second. In snapdragons, red petals need an enzyme that helps make red pigment. Two plants each carry two copies of a different change in this enzyme's gene. In plant P, the mRNA codon for an amino acid in the active site changes from C A U to C C U. In plant Q, a codon far from the active site changes from G A A to G A G. Plant P has white flowers, and plant Q has red flowers. Use the chart to explain both. Pause here to answer.

In plant P, C A U is histidine and C C U is proline, so a different amino acid sits in the active site. The pocket's shape changes, the enzyme can't hold its substrate, and no red pigment forms, so the flowers are white. In plant Q, G A A and G A G both code for glutamate, so the enzyme is unchanged and the flowers stay red. If you said every change to a gene changes the protein, check the chart first.

So when a question links a gene to a trait, walk the chain: the base, the codon, the amino acid, the shape, what the cell does, then the trait. And when the same genes give different results, look for what the environment is changing. Next, where the different genotypes in one family come from in the first place.
